key_facts: **Alopecia areata** is autoimmune, **non-scarring** hair loss in round or oval patches with normal-looking skin.
**Exclamation-mark hairs** at the edge; can affect beard, brows, lashes and nails (pitting).
Severe forms: **ophiasis** (band along the hairline), totalis (whole scalp) and universalis (all body hair).
About 80% of small, short-duration patches regrow within a year, but relapse is common.
Adults: potent or very potent scalp steroid for about 3 months (off-label); refer children, extensive or distressing disease (JAK inhibitors are specialist).

sections.title: Overview
blocks: **Alopecia areata (AA)** is a common autoimmune **non-scarring** hair loss causing sudden smooth bald patches on any hair-bearing site. Lifetime risk is about 2%. Spectrum: patchy AA, ophiasis, diffuse AA, **alopecia totalis** (all scalp) and **universalis** (all body hair).

sub: Lifetime risk about 2%; any age, often starting in childhood or young adulthood.
Associated with atopy, thyroid disease, vitiligo and Down syndrome.

ul: Collapse of hair-follicle immune privilege → peribulbar T-cell attack; IFN-γ/IL-15 via JAK–STAT (rationale for specialist JAK inhibitors).
Genetic predisposition (~1 in 5 family history). Triggers sometimes cited: stress, illness — often none found.
Associations: autoimmune thyroid disease, vitiligo, type 1 diabetes, atopy, Down syndrome; higher anxiety/depression rates.
Loss of the hair follicle's **immune privilege** with CD8+ T-cell attack; genetic susceptibility (HLA, ULBP3).
Triggers sometimes reported: stress, illness.
**"Stress alone causes it"**: it is autoimmune; stress may trigger flares.
**"Hair loss is permanent"**: follicles are not destroyed, so regrowth is possible even after years.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: Immune cells attack **growing (anagen) hair bulbs** but spare the stem cells, so hair can regrow.

mech.t: Anagen bulbs normally hide their antigens (low MHC class I); in AA this privilege fails.
Interferon-γ and **JAK–STAT** signalling recruit CD8+ T cells around the bulb ('swarm of bees'): the target of JAK inhibitors.
Damaged hairs narrow near the scalp and break: **exclamation-mark hairs**; follicles enter early catagen and telogen.
Stem cells in the bulge survive, so regrowth often starts as fine white hairs that later repigment.

histo: Peribulbar lymphocytic infiltrate around anagen follicles; increased catagen/telogen hairs; no scarring. Biopsy only if the diagnosis is uncertain.

ul: Round/oval smooth skin-coloured patches; **no scale, erythema or scarring**; ostia preserved.
**Exclamation-mark hairs** at active margins; pull test positive at the edge.
Grey/white hairs often spared; regrowth may start as fine white vellus hairs.
Nail **pitting** (thimble pits); also trachyonychia.
May involve brows, lashes and beard — avoid potent topical steroids on the face.

sub: Refer; use lower-potency steroids, and consider the psychosocial impact and school support.
Fine regular pitting or trachyonychia in 10–20%, more with severe disease.

ul: Clinical: extent, speed, prior episodes, autoimmune/atopy history, psychosocial impact.
Trichoscopy: exclamation marks, yellow dots (ostia present), black dots, tapered/regrowing hairs.
Mycology if scale or childhood doubt (exclude tinea). Syphilis serology if moth-eaten. ANA if lupus possible.
Thyroid: consider TSH ± TPO especially in totalis/universalis or symptoms; check TSH is in range if already hypothyroid (coexistent telogen effluvium).
Routine iron/zinc/vitamin D supplementation is not evidence-based for AA (BAD).

ddx.f: Diffuse shed; trigger 2–3 months earlier — see [telogen effluvium](condition:telogen-effluvium)

ddx.name: Scarring alopecia
ddx.f: Lost ostia, shiny scalp, symptoms — see [scarring alopecia](condition:scarring-alopecia)

ul: Explain unpredictability; ~80% of limited short-duration patches regrow within a year, but relapses are common. Extensive/AT/AU: full recovery ~1 in 10.
Sun protection on bald patches; signpost Alopecia UK / BAD leaflets; screen psychological distress.
**No treatment / watchful waiting** if already regrowing or small non-distressing patches.
Adults: potent or very potent **scalp** steroid once daily for about **3 months** (off-label); reassess 3–6 months. Never potent steroid on face/brows.
Camouflage, fibres, brows/lashes cosmetics; NHS wigs need a dermatologist’s prescription.

refer.t: Childhood scaly patch → treat/investigate as tinea.
Lost follicular openings / symptoms of scarring → urgent derm.
Significant distress, school withdrawal, self-harm risk → mental-health pathways.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Childhood scaly patch → treat/investigate as tinea.
Lost follicular openings / symptoms of scarring → urgent derm.
Significant distress, school withdrawal, self-harm risk → mental-health pathways.

Child, pregnancy/breastfeeding, diagnostic doubt, severe/rapid progression (ophiasis, AT/AU), no response at 3–6 months, major psychosocial impact, facial-site treatment wanted, or wig prescription needed.
Specialist options (counsel only): intralesional steroid, contact immunotherapy, JAK inhibitors, systemic agents — do not initiate without training/pathway.
Anxiety, depression and social withdrawal.
Loss of eyelashes and brows (eye irritation).
Associated autoimmune disease.
Unpredictable. Worse outlook: onset in childhood, extensive or ophiasis pattern, nail disease, atopy, long duration.

pearls: Yellow dots on trichoscopy prove follicles are still there — hope for regrowth.
Regrowth takes months and may be white at first — set expectations.
Check TSH is optimised if the patient is already on thyroxine.

quiz.q: When should you think of Alopecia areata?
quiz.a: Sudden smooth round bald patch without scale or scarring; exclamation-mark hairs at the active edge; nails may be pitted.
CD8+ T-cell attack on the anagen bulb (JAK–STAT); stem-cell bulge spared → non-scarring and potentially reversible.

quiz.q: What is the backbone of care?
quiz.a: Explain and support; watchful waiting or potent scalp steroid for 3 months in adults; camouflage/wigs; refer severe, childhood or non-responding disease.
Scaly childhood patch = tinea until proven otherwise. Loss of follicular ostia = scarring alopecia — urgent dermatology.

quiz.q: Name a red flag that needs escalation.
quiz.a: Childhood scaly patch → treat/investigate as tinea.
